lessons.title: Allah in the Qur'an: Al-Fatiha, Tawhid and the 99 Names

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that Surah al-Fatiha (Surah 1) teaches Muslims about Allah.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Allah is the Lord of all worlds — he has authority over and created all that exists.
• Allah is both Ar-Rahman (universally merciful) and Ar-Rahim (specifically merciful to believers) — mercy is his defining characteristic.
• Allah is the Master of the Day of Judgement — all will ultimately be accountable to him.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Tawhid means and why it is central to Islamic belief.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Tawhid means the absolute oneness and uniqueness of Allah — there is no god but Allah.
• It rules out all partners, equals, offspring or rivals to Allah — ascribing partners is the greatest sin (shirk).
• It is expressed in the Shahadah: 'There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is his messenger', which every Muslim recites.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the 99 names of Allah help Muslims understand who Allah is.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• The name Al-Khaliq (the Creator) tells Muslims that Allah is the sole originator of all things — nothing in creation made itself, and this gives human life meaning and purpose as part of Allah's deliberate creation.
• The name Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) tells Muslims that Allah continually covers and forgives sin for those who repent — this shapes Muslim prayer practice, encouraging honest confession and trust in divine forgiveness.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two differences between the names Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Ar-Rahman refers to Allah's universal, overflowing mercy — it is extended to all creation, believer and non-believer alike, sustaining the world in existence. It is found in Surah 55:1 ('Ar-Rahman — He taught the Qur'an').
• Ar-Rahim refers to the specific mercy Allah shows particularly to believers — the mercy of forgiveness, spiritual reward, and paradise for those who submit to his will. It is found in Surah 3:31.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 55:1 (for Ar-Rahman) or Surah 3:31 (for Ar-Rahim) as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Tawhid is the foundational belief — without it, no other Islamic practice makes sense. The Shahadah (declaration of faith) begins with Tawhid. Shirk (associating partners with Allah) is described in the Qur'an as the one sin that cannot be forgiven if died upon. Every Five Pillar is an expression of Tawhid — directing worship and obedience to Allah alone.
Against: Some Muslims might argue prophethood (Risalah) is equally foundational — without the Prophet Muhammad, the Qur'an would not have been revealed and Tawhid itself would not be known. Others might argue the Day of Judgement (Akhirah) is the most practically motivating belief, since it shapes daily ethical choices. Non-religious thinkers would question whether any religious belief is 'important' in an objective sense, arguing that ethics and compassion are what truly matter.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the 99 names of Allah are important for Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Muslims use the names in dhikr (remembrance) — reciting them with prayer beads deepens their knowledge of and love for Allah.
• The names shape Islamic ethics: because Allah is Ar-Razzaq (the Sustainer), Muslims are encouraged to be generous with wealth, knowing it ultimately comes from Allah.
• Specific names are called upon in different types of prayer: Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) in prayers for forgiveness, As-Salam (the Source of Peace) in prayers for comfort.

before.exam_tip_html: For 5-mark “Explain two with sources” questions on the names of Allah, you must cite the surah reference to earn the fifth mark. For example: “The name Al-Khaliq means ‘the Creator’. In Surah 6:102, Allah is described as the Creator of all things…” — that final reference earns the mark. Don’t paraphrase without the surah number. For 12-mark Discuss questions on Tawhid or the nature of Allah, show you understand Islamic diversity: Sunni and Shi’a both affirm Tawhid but may describe it differently (Shi’a theology adds Adl — divine justice). For SPaG, correctly spell ‘Tawhid’, ‘Bismillah’ and ‘Ar-Rahman’; capitalise the names of Allah.
before.content_html:
Al-Fatiha: The Opening of the Qur’an

Surah al-Fatiha (Surah 1) is the first chapter of the Qur’an and its spiritual heart. Its name means “the Opening.” It consists of seven verses and is recited in every raka’a (unit) of the daily prayer — meaning a devout Muslim recites it at least seventeen times a day. It begins: “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.” This opening formula, known as the Bismillah, begins 113 of the 114 surahs of the Qur’an.

Al-Fatiha moves through praise of Allah as Lord of all worlds, the Gracious and the Merciful, the Master of the Day of Judgement, before turning to a declaration of total dependence: “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.” It closes with a petition to be guided on “the straight path” — the path of those Allah has blessed, not those who have gone astray.

For Muslims, al-Fatiha is a summary of the whole Qur’an in miniature: it establishes who Allah is (the Lord, the Merciful), what the human relationship with Allah should be (worship and dependence), and what the goal of human life is (guidance on the straight path, leading ultimately to the bliss of paradise). Its brevity and comprehensiveness make it uniquely powerful as a daily act of worship.

Tawhid: The Oneness of Allah

The central theological concept of Islam is Tawhid. It means that Allah is one — absolutely and uniquely. This is not simply numerical oneness (the idea that there is one God rather than many) but a qualitative uniqueness: nothing in creation can be compared to Allah, nothing shares his divine nature, and he has no partners, no equals, no offspring and no rivals.

Surah al-Anaam (Surah 6), verses 13–24, expresses this powerfully. It condemns those who “ascribe partners to Allah” and affirms that everything in heaven and earth belongs to him. Allah is described as the Knower of hidden and open things, as the Master of everything. For Muslims, belief in Tawhid shapes every aspect of life: it means that ultimate loyalty belongs to Allah alone, that no human authority can override divine command, and that every act of worship must be directed to Allah and no one else.

Key Fact

Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah — is Islam’s foundational belief. The Shahadah (the declaration of faith) expresses it: “There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is his messenger.” Every Islamic practice flows from Tawhid: prayer is directed to Allah alone, shirk (ascribing partners to Allah) is the gravest sin, and all other beliefs are orientated around this central affirmation of divine uniqueness.

The 99 Beautiful Names of Allah

The Qur’an refers to Allah by many names and attributes. Muslim tradition identifies 99 of these as the 99 Beautiful Names (Asma ul-Husna). Each name is both a description of Allah’s nature and a guide to how believers should relate to him. Reciting the names is itself a form of worship — the Prophet Muhammad is reported to have said that Allah has 99 names, and whoever memorises them will enter paradise. The specification focuses on six specific names, each anchored in a Qur’anic verse.

Ar-Rahman (Surah 55:1) — the All-Merciful. This name refers to Allah’s universal, overflowing mercy that extends to all creation, believer and non-believer alike. It is the mercy that sustains the world in existence, the mercy behind creation itself. Ar-Rahim (Surah 3:31) — also translated “the All-Merciful,” but with a different shade: where Ar-Rahman is broad and universal, Ar-Rahim refers to the specific, particular mercy Allah shows to believers who turn to him. Both names open al-Fatiha, establishing that Allah’s fundamental character is merciful.

As-Salam (Surah 59:23) — the Source of Peace. Allah is not simply at peace; he is the source and origin of all peace. The Arabic greeting “as-salamu alaykum” (peace be upon you) derives from this same root, connecting everyday Muslim social life to the divine attribute. Al-Khaliq (Surah 6:102) — the Creator. Allah alone is the originator of all things. Nothing in creation created itself; everything owes its existence to Allah’s creative act. This name underpins the Islamic doctrine of creation.

Al-Ghaffar (Surah 2:173) — the All-Forgiving, or the One who repeatedly forgives. This name emphasises that Allah’s forgiveness is not a single act but a continuous attribute — he covers and forgives sins again and again for those who sincerely repent. Ar-Razzaq (Surah 51:58) — the Sustainer, or the One who provides. Allah is the provider of all sustenance — physical food, spiritual nourishment, and everything a creature needs. This name encourages Muslims to trust Allah’s provision and to be generous, since ultimately all wealth comes from him.

Both Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim come from the Arabic root r-h-m, related to the word for womb (rahim) — suggesting mercy that is as fundamental and enveloping as a mother’s care for a child.

The distinction: Ar-Rahman (active participle, intensive) expresses Allah’s ongoing, universal mercy — the mercy that creates the world, provides rain, and sustains all life regardless of belief. It is often said that Ar-Rahman is exclusively an attribute of Allah — it cannot be used as a name for a human being. Ar-Rahim (intensive adjectival form) expresses the specific mercy Allah directs towards believers who turn to him in faith and repentance. While Ar-Rahman covers the whole creation, Ar-Rahim is the mercy of the hereafter, the reward of the faithful.

Together, the two names at the start of al-Fatiha — and at the start of virtually every surah — announce that the God who speaks in the Qur’an is, before everything else, a God of mercy.

Key Fact

The six specified names with their Qur’anic anchors: Ar-Rahman = universal mercy (Surah 55:1); Ar-Rahim = specific mercy for believers (Surah 3:31); As-Salam = Source of Peace (Surah 59:23); Al-Khaliq = the Creator (Surah 6:102); Al-Ghaffar = the All-Forgiving (Surah 2:173); Ar-Razzaq = the Sustainer (Surah 51:58). Knowing the name, meaning and surah reference is the full exam answer for the 5-mark source question.

Muslims recite the 99 names using prayer beads (subha or tasbih) in a practice called dhikr (remembrance of Allah). Repeating the names is itself an act of worship — meditating on each name deepens understanding of who Allah is and how to relate to him. Different names are called upon in different contexts: Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) is invoked in prayer for forgiveness; Ar-Razzaq (the Sustainer) in prayers for provision; As-Salam (the Source of Peace) in prayers for peace of heart.

The names also shape Islamic ethics: because Allah is As-Salam, Muslims are called to be instruments of peace; because Allah is Al-Ghaffar, Muslims are encouraged to be forgiving; because Allah is Ar-Razzaq and provides all sustenance, Muslims are encouraged to give generously to those in need. The 99 names are not just theology — they are a programme for living.

lessons.title: Believers, Creation and Humanity as Khalifah

practice_questions.text: Outline three characteristics of the believer as described in Surah al-Baqarah.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Believers believe in the unseen — they trust in Allah, angels, and the hereafter without direct sensory proof.
• They establish regular prayer (salah) — their faith is expressed through structured, daily acts of worship.
• They give from what Allah has provided — their belief is shown in generosity and care for others.

practice_questions.text: Describe the story of Adam as khalifah in Surah 2:30-39.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Allah announced to the angels that he would create a vicegerent (khalifah) on earth; the angels questioned this because humans would cause corruption.
• Adam was taught the names of all things and the angels were commanded to bow to him — all did except Iblis, who refused.
• Adam and his wife were placed in a garden, tempted by Iblis, and sent to earth when they disobeyed; Allah forgave Adam when he repented.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Qur'anic creation account shows what Allah is like.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Creation demonstrates Allah's absolute power — the concept of Kun fa-yakun ('Be! And it is') in passages like Surah 41:11 shows that Allah creates simply by speaking; nothing can resist or limit his creative command.
• Creation is a sign pointing to Allah — Surah 45:3-5 describes the alternation of night and day, the provision of rain and the diversity of creation as signs for 'people of understanding'; Allah communicates his existence through the natural world.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the concept of khalifah affects how Muslims live today.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Khalifah means Muslims see themselves as stewards of the earth, not its owners — they are accountable to Allah for how they treat the environment, giving Islamic support for conservation and opposition to wasteful consumption.
• Khalifah also extends to social justice: as stewards, Muslims are responsible for the fair distribution of wealth and care for the vulnerable — this connects to the payment of zakah and the commitment to justice found throughout Surah 2.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 2:30 (or the khalifah passage) as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The Qur'anic teaching that humans are khalifah is the most important teaching about human beings in Islam.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Khalifah establishes humanity's unique relationship with Allah — above the angels (who bowed to Adam), trusted with the earth, accountable at Judgement. It underpins both environmental ethics and social justice in Islam. The passage (Surah 2:30-39) is foundational for understanding human dignity and responsibility.
Against: Some would argue the doctrine of Tawhid is more fundamental — without understanding who Allah is, the concept of human stewardship has no context. Others might argue the Five Pillars are the most important expression of what it means to be human in Islam — they define the practical shape of Muslim life. Non-religious thinkers would question any teaching that grants humans a unique divine-given role, arguing that humans are simply one species among many with no special mandate.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which Surah al-Baqarah describes non-believers and hypocrites.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Non-believers are described as having 'sealed hearts' — they will not respond to warning because they have hardened themselves against truth.
• Their hearing and sight are described as covered — they cannot receive the message of the Qur'an.
• Hypocrites claim to believe but do not — the Qur'an treats them as more dangerous than open unbelievers because they corrupt the community from within.

before.exam_tip_html: For “Explain two with sources” questions on creation or khalifah, cite the surah reference: “In Surah 2:30, Allah announces ‘I will create a vicegerent on earth’…” gives you the source mark. For 12-mark Discuss questions, the angles question (non-religious view) might challenge whether the creation account is scientific or simply mythological — develop the Muslim response fully, including how Qur’anic creation is read as sign rather than scientific textbook. Remember to distinguish Surah al-Baqarah (Surah 2) from other surahs — it is the longest surah and contains many different topics. SPaG: spell ‘khalifah’ (or ‘vicegerent’) and ‘Bismillah’ correctly; use ‘Iblis’ (not ‘Shaytan’) when referring to Surah 2’s account.
before.content_html:
Believers and Non-Believers in Surah al-Baqarah

Surah al-Baqarah (Surah 2) is the longest chapter in the Qur’an and one of the most important. Its name, meaning “the Cow,” refers to the story of Moses and a miraculous cow in verses 67–73. The surah opens with a description of three groups of people, presenting a moral map of humanity from the Qur’an’s perspective.

Those who believe are described as people who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, give from what Allah has provided, believe in what was revealed to Muhammad and in earlier revelations, and are certain of the hereafter. For them, the Qur’an says, “such are on guidance from their Lord and such are the successful.” Their faith is active: it manifests in prayer, generosity and moral seriousness, not merely in intellectual assent.

Those who disbelieve are described as people for whom warning makes no difference — their hearts are sealed, their hearing and sight are covered. This language uses the Qur’anic concept of the “sealed heart” — not a physical sealing but a description of a state of moral hardening caused by repeated rejection of truth. A third group, the hypocrites, claim to believe but do not. The Qur’an treats hypocrisy as more dangerous than open disbelief, because it corrupts the community from within.

Key Fact

In Surah al-Baqarah, the believer is someone who: (1) believes in the unseen, (2) establishes prayer, (3) gives from what Allah has provided. Their faith is not passive — it is expressed through worship, generosity and moral action. This portrait of the believer shapes Islamic practice: faith and action cannot be separated.

The Qur’anic Account of Creation

The Qur’an does not give a single unified creation narrative like Genesis 1–2. Instead, creation references are spread across many surahs, each emphasising a different aspect. Several key verses are specified. In Surah 21:30, Allah declares: “Do not the unbelievers see that the heavens and the earth were joined together (as one unit of creation), before We clove them asunder?” This verse is often cited in discussions of whether the Qur’an anticipates modern scientific theories about the origins of the universe. Muslim scholars debate the significance of this verse in relation to cosmology.

Surah 41:11 describes Allah addressing the heavens while they were “smoke” and commanding them and the earth to come into existence willingly or unwillingly — they replied: “We come, in willing obedience.” This passage emphasises that creation is an act of divine command (the Qur’anic concept of Kun fa-yakun — “Be! And it is”). Surah 7:54 states that Allah created the heavens and earth in six “days” (the Arabic word ayyam can mean periods or eras rather than 24-hour days) and then “established himself on the Throne”.

In Surah 45:3–5, creation itself is presented as a sign (ayah) of Allah’s existence and power: the alternation of night and day, the provision of rain, the diversity of languages and colours — all are described as signs “for people of understanding.” This approach — reading the natural world as a testimony to Allah — is a central feature of Qur’anic theology. The universe is not an accident but a deliberate act of communication from the Creator.

Humanity as Khalifah: Surah 2:30–39

One of the most important theological concepts in the Qur’an about human beings is the idea of khalifah. In Surah 2:30–39, Allah announces to the angels: “I will create a vicegerent on earth.” The word khalifah means successor, steward or vicegerent — someone who acts on behalf of another. The angels protest: “Will you place therein one who will spread corruption and shed blood while we glorify your praise?” Allah replies: “I know what you do not know.”

Adam is then created and taught the names of all things — a privilege not given to the angels. When Adam demonstrates this knowledge, Allah commands the angels to bow to Adam. They all do, except Iblis, who refuses out of pride. Iblis becomes the tempter of humanity. Adam and his wife are placed in the garden but warned not to eat from one tree; Iblis deceives them, they eat, and they are sent to live on earth. Allah, however, forgives Adam when he repents — showing that human beings are created weak but capable of repentance and restoration.

The concept of khalifah has profound ethical implications. If humanity is Allah’s steward on earth, then human beings are accountable for how they treat the environment, other creatures and other people. They are trustees, not owners. This forms the Qur’anic basis for environmental ethics in Islam — the earth belongs to Allah, and humans must care for it accordingly.

Both the Qur’an and the Bible present creation as the deliberate act of one God, who creates humanity with a special status above other creatures. Both have a story of a garden, a temptation, a fall and expulsion. Both use six “days” or periods of creation.

Key differences: In the Qur’anic account, Adam repents and is forgiven — there is no concept of “original sin” passed to all humanity. In Islamic theology, human beings are born in a state of fitrah (natural purity) rather than sinfulness. The Qur’an does not name Adam’s wife in these passages. Responsibility for the disobedience is shared more equally between Adam and his wife in the Qur’an than in some readings of Genesis 3, where the woman is often held more responsible.

Modern Muslim scholars and activists draw on the concept of khalifah to argue for Islamic environmental ethics. If humanity is entrusted with the earth as Allah’s steward, then environmental destruction is a form of betrayal of that trust — a spiritual as well as an ethical failure. The Islamic Foundation for Ecology and Environmental Sciences (IFEES) has developed this theology in practical work on conservation.

The concept of khalifah also extends to social justice: as stewards, humans are accountable for how they treat the poor, the marginalised and the oppressed. The same Surah 2 that establishes the believer’s identity also contains laws on just economic dealings, care for orphans and widows, and the payment of zakah (almsgiving). Stewardship is both environmental and social.

Key Fact

Khalifah means vicegerent, steward or successor. In Surah 2:30–39, Allah appoints humanity as his khalifah on earth. This means human beings are trustees, not owners, of the natural world — accountable to Allah for how they treat creation. This is the Qur’anic basis for Islamic environmental ethics and social justice.

glossary_terms.definition: Surah 2 — the longest surah in the Qur'an, covering laws, beliefs and stories of earlier prophets; its name means 'The Cow'.
People described in the Qur'an as saying they believe but whose faith is insincere; also called hypocrites.
Surah 21, 'The Prophets'; verse 30 describes the heavens and earth as once joined together before Allah separated them.
The divine command 'Be!' by which Allah creates; from Arabic meaning 'to be', expressing Allah's absolute creative power.
Successor, steward or vicegerent; in Surah 2:30, Allah tells the angels he will place a khalifah on earth, understood as humanity acting as his steward and representative.
A jinn (spirit being) who refused to bow to Adam because of pride; the Islamic equivalent of Satan.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that the Qur'an teaches about justice in Surah An-Nisa.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Surah 4:135 commands Muslims to stand firmly for justice even against themselves, their parents or their relatives.
• Justice must be impartial — it should not favour the rich over the poor or the powerful over the weak.
• Justice is grounded in Allah's own character as Al-'Adl (the Just) — because Allah is just, humans are required to be just as his stewards on earth.

practice_questions.text: Describe what shirk means and why it is considered so serious in Islam.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Shirk means associating partners with Allah — giving to any created thing the worship or ultimate loyalty that belongs to Allah alone.
• It is the opposite of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and is considered the one sin that cannot be forgiven if persisted in until death.
• The Qur'an condemns idolatry as a form of shirk — Surah 7:148-150 illustrates this with the golden calf story.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Shari'ah law is important for Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Shari'ah provides a comprehensive guide to worship and personal conduct — daily prayer, fasting, halal food laws and zakah are all part of Shari'ah, giving Muslim life a coherent, God-centred structure that goes beyond merely following human custom.
• Shari'ah provides a framework for justice and ethics — its principles of fairness, care for the vulnerable and prohibition of exploitation are applied in Muslim communities around the world, whether in full legal systems or in personal ethical choices.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the teaching about shirk shapes how Muslims live today.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Shirk shapes Muslim worship: because ascribing partners to Allah is forbidden, all prayer and devotion must be directed to Allah alone — no image, statue or mediating figure can be the object of worship. This is why mosques are adorned with geometric patterns and calligraphy rather than images of Allah or the prophets.
• Shirk shapes Muslim responses to other religions: Islam's insistence on Tawhid means Muslims cannot accept Trinitarian Christianity or Hindu polytheism as fully valid, though they recognise the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) as having received earlier revelation from Allah.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 7:148-150 (golden calf) or another shirk-related passage as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Following Shari'ah law is unnecessary for Muslims living in modern Britain.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support (of the statement): Humanists argue that ethics should be based on human reason and democratic consent, not divine commands. Some Shari'ah rulings developed in 7th-century Arabia may not be appropriate for 21st-century Britain. Muslims in Britain live under civil law, which already provides frameworks for justice and rights. Following Shari'ah in all details would create two parallel legal systems.
Against: The Qur'an commands obedience to Allah and the Messenger (Surah 4:59) — for committed Muslims, Shari'ah is not optional but an expression of submission to Allah. Even in Britain, Muslims observe many aspects of Shari'ah (prayer times, halal food, fasting, family law in some cases). Many Muslim scholars argue Shari'ah's principles of justice, compassion and care for the vulnerable are entirely compatible with modern life. The Sunnah (Surah 33:21-36) provides the model for how Shari'ah is lived — adaptable to context while rooted in divine guidance.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the golden calf story in Surah 7:148-150 illustrates the problem of shirk.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• The Israelites made and worshipped a physical image in Moses's absence — this substituted a visible, created thing for the invisible, eternal God.
• The calf could not speak, guide or help its worshippers — this shows the Qur'an's argument that idols are powerless compared to Allah.
• Moses's anger on his return demonstrates how seriously shirk is treated — it is a betrayal of the covenant relationship with Allah.

before.exam_tip_html: For 5-mark questions on Shari’ah, name a surah reference: “In Surah 4:59, Allah commands obedience to himself, the Messenger and those in authority…” earns the source mark. For questions on shirk, you can use Surah 7:148–150 (the golden calf) as your source. For 12-mark Discuss questions on Shari’ah being ‘unnecessary in modern society,’ develop the Humanist/atheist argument fully (democratic consent, human rights tensions) before presenting the Muslim response — the most common failure is treating the opposing view as a single dismissive sentence. SPaG: spell ‘Shari’ah’ with the apostrophe and the ‘h’ at the end; spell ‘shirk’ in lower case (it is a common noun, not a proper name). Use ‘Adl’ when referring to divine justice in Shi’a Islam.
before.content_html:
Justice in Surah An-Nisa (Surah 4:105–135)

Surah An-Nisa (Surah 4, “The Women”) is one of the longest chapters in the Qur’an and covers a wide range of legal and social teachings. Verses 105–135 focus particularly on justice. The Qur’an’s vision of justice is comprehensive — it covers legal fairness in courts, economic fairness, treatment of the poor, and the rights of women, orphans and prisoners.

In Surah 4:135, Allah commands: “O you who believe! Stand out firmly for justice, as witnesses to Allah, even if it be against yourselves, your parents, or your relatives, or whether it be against the rich or the poor.” This is a demanding standard — justice must be impartial even when it is personally costly. A Muslim is expected to testify truthfully even against their own family.

The Qur’an also connects justice to the character of Allah. Because Allah is Just (Al-‘Adl, one of the 99 names), human beings as his khalifah on earth are required to mirror that justice in their institutions and relationships. In Shi’a Islam, Adl (divine justice) is one of the Five Roots of faith, making it even more central to that tradition’s theology.

The Hadith traditions also illustrate justice in practice. The Prophet Muhammad’s recorded sayings and actions (Hadith) show him returning stolen goods, insisting that even a powerful person should be punished for wrongdoing, and declaring that “whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy.” These traditions show justice as lived, practical and applied, not merely theological.

Key Fact

Surah 4:135 commands Muslims to “stand out firmly for justice… even if it be against yourselves, your parents, or your relatives.” This makes justice a binding obligation that overrides personal loyalty. It connects to the Islamic concept of Adl (divine justice) — because Allah is Just, Muslims must be just even at personal cost.

Shirk: The Greatest Sin

Shirk means to ascribe partners to Allah — to associate anything or anyone with his divine nature. It is the opposite of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and is considered the gravest sin in Islam. The Qur’an states repeatedly that Allah may forgive any sin except shirk for those who die without repenting.

Shirk takes several forms. The most obvious is idol worship — worshipping statues or images as gods. Surah 7:148–150 recounts the story of the Israelites who made and worshipped a golden calf while Moses was receiving the Torah on Sinai. Moses returned to find the people in this act of shirk and was furious. The story is a vivid illustration of how easily human beings fall into substituting a visible, created thing for the invisible, eternal God.

More subtle forms of shirk include: placing ultimate trust or fear in human beings or institutions rather than Allah; following desires (the “lower self”) as if they were divine commands; and giving to human relationships the devotion that belongs only to Allah. Muslim scholars have also identified “hidden shirk” — performing religious acts for human approval rather than sincerely for Allah.

For Muslims today, the condemnation of shirk shapes their approach to other religions. Some Muslim scholars argue that Christian Trinitarian theology — which speaks of God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit — approaches shirk by attributing a partner (Jesus) to Allah. Most Muslims, however, engage respectfully with Christians and Jews as “People of the Book,” recognising the partial truth in their scriptures while maintaining the Islamic insistence on strict divine unity.

The story of the golden calf in Surah 7:148–150 parallels the account in Exodus 32 but with some differences. In the Qur’anic version, the Israelites made the calf in Moses’s absence and worshipped it; they “could not see that it could not speak to them or guide them any way.” Moses returned, cast down the calf and rebuked his brother Aaron for allowing it. The idols’ inability to speak, guide or help their worshippers is a recurring Qur’anic argument against idolatry: only Allah can respond, guide and provide.

The story teaches that shirk is a moral as well as a theological failure — it involves a refusal to reason carefully about what is worthy of worship. The Qur’an repeatedly challenges idol-worshippers to explain how a created thing can have divine attributes. Ibrahim’s famous destruction of his people’s idols (discussed in a later lesson) makes the same point with dramatic action.

Shari’ah Law

Shari’ah means “path” or “way” in Arabic — the path that Allah has revealed for human beings to follow. It is not simply a legal code but a comprehensive guide to how a Muslim should live in relationship with Allah, with other people, and with the natural world. Shari’ah covers worship (ibadat), relationships and family (muamalat), criminal law (uqubat), and social ethics.

Surah 4:59–60 is one of the foundational Qur’anic verses for Shari’ah: “O you who believe! Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you disagree about anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger.” This verse establishes the hierarchy of Islamic legal authority: first the Qur’an (Allah), then the Sunnah (the Prophet’s practice and sayings), then the rulings of qualified scholars.

Surah 33:21–36 reinforces the idea that the Prophet Muhammad is the model for the Muslim community. Verse 21 states: “Certainly you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example.” This is the Qur’anic basis for the Sunnah as a source of Islamic law alongside the Qur’an — if you want to know how to live, look at how the Prophet lived.

From an atheist or Humanist perspective, following a religious legal code such as Shari’ah is problematic for several reasons. First, they would argue that laws should derive from democratic consent and human reason, not from texts claimed to be divine revelation. Second, they might point to specific rulings in classical Shari’ah (on gender equality, religious freedom, or punishments) that appear in tension with modern human rights standards. Third, they would question the principle that God’s command is a sufficient basis for law without independent moral justification.

Muslims respond in a number of ways. Many distinguish between the unchanging core of Shari’ah (the principles of justice, compassion and care for the vulnerable) and the specific rulings that were developed in a historical context and can be reinterpreted. Modern Muslim scholars such as Tariq Ramadan argue that Shari’ah is best understood as an ethical framework rather than a rigid legal code. Muslims in democratic societies typically observe the personal dimensions of Shari’ah (prayer, fasting, halal food) while living under civil law.

Key Fact

Shari’ah means “path” — the comprehensive guide to Muslim life. Its sources are the Qur’an and the Sunnah (the Prophet’s practice). Surah 4:59 establishes the hierarchy: “Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority.” Shari’ah covers worship, family, ethics and legal matters, and is understood differently by different Muslim communities around the world.

lessons.title: The Prophets: Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail and Yusuf

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that Surah 71 (Nuh) teaches about the Prophet Nuh.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Nuh preached to his people for a very long time, calling them day and night, publicly and privately — showing great perseverance in the face of repeated rejection.
• His people refused to listen, mocking him and blocking their ears — only a small group believed.
• Allah commanded Nuh to build the Ark; after the flood he was called a 'grateful servant' (shakur) in Surah 17:3.

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Qur'an says about Ibrahim and Ismail building the Ka'ba (Surah 2:127-129).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Ibrahim and Ismail together raised the foundations of the Ka'ba in Makkah.
• They prayed: 'Our Lord, accept this service from us' — asking Allah to receive their act of worship.
• They prayed for their descendants to be a Muslim community and asked Allah to 'send among them a messenger' — a prayer Muslims see as fulfilled in the Prophet Muhammad.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the story of the Prophet Yusuf (Surah 12) is important for Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Yusuf's patience through betrayal, slavery and imprisonment shows that trusting Allah even in extreme suffering brings ultimate vindication — his story encourages Muslims to maintain faith and integrity when life is unjust.
• Yusuf's forgiveness of his brothers ('No reproach on you this day; Allah forgives you') models Islamic values of forgiveness and reconciliation, showing that forgiving those who have wronged you is a sign of closeness to Allah.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the story of Ibrahim in the Qur'an shows what it means to submit to Allah.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Ibrahim's destruction of the idols (Surah 21:57-58) shows that submission to Allah requires rejection of all false gods — even when his own community and family worshipped them, he acted on his rational recognition that created objects cannot be divine.
• Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son (Surah 37:99-111) represents the ultimate test of submission — he placed obedience to Allah above even his natural love for his child; the intervention of Allah (providing an animal instead) confirmed that his submission was accepted.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 21:57-58 or Surah 37:109-111 as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The story of Ibrahim is the most important prophet story in the Qur'an.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Ibrahim is described as 'Friend of Allah' (Khalilullah) — a unique honour. He is the ancestor of the Prophet Muhammad through Ismail. He built the Ka'ba — Islam's most sacred site. His willingness to sacrifice his son is commemorated in Id-ul-Adha, one of the two great Muslim festivals. He is the model of rational faith that rejects idolatry.
Against: Surah 12 calls Yusuf's story 'the best of stories' — suggesting it has a unique quality of narrative depth and moral richness. Nuh is described in Surah 17:3 as a 'grateful servant' — a profound model of perseverance. Muhammad is described as the Seal of the Prophets and is the one who received the final, complete revelation — in that sense the most important. Non-religious observers might question the entire concept of prophetic authority, arguing that moral wisdom does not need to be divinely authorised.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the Prophet Nuh's story is similar to or different from the Bible's account of Noah.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point (similarity or difference):
• Both the Qur'an and the Bible describe Nuh/Noah building an ark at God's command to survive a flood — the basic structure of the story is shared.
• In the Qur'an (unlike Genesis), Nuh's own son drowns in the flood because he refuses to believe — this detail is unique to the Qur'anic account.
• Both accounts describe Nuh/Noah as a righteous man chosen by God for his faithfulness in a corrupt generation.

before.content_html:
The Prophets in Islam

In Islam, Allah has sent a series of prophets to guide humanity. All share the same core message: submit to Allah, worship him alone, and live justly. Each prophet faces opposition, suffers for his message, and ultimately depends on Allah rather than human approval. The Qur’an’s prophet stories are not simply biographical — they are theological templates for how every believer should respond to Allah’s call.

The Prophet Nuh (Noah)

Nuh is one of the earliest prophets in Islamic tradition. He is described in Surah 17:3 as a “grateful servant” (shakur) — his defining characteristic is thankfulness to Allah even when his mission was almost entirely rejected. Surah 71 (Nuh) is devoted entirely to his story. He preached to his people for 950 years (a figurative number expressing the duration of his mission). He called them day and night, publicly and privately, offering them forgiveness if they would turn to Allah.

They refused. They mocked him. They blocked their ears and put their fingers in them so as not to hear. Only a small group believed. Allah then commanded Nuh to build the Ark. The flood came, destroying the rest — including Nuh’s own son, who refused to board the ark and drowned. This detail is unique to the Qur’anic account: Nuh’s son is separated from him by his disbelief, and Allah tells Nuh that the son is not “of your family” because his actions were not righteous. Faith, not biology, defines the community of Allah.

After the flood, Nuh is told to disembark with “peace and blessing from us on you and on some of the peoples who will descend from you.” His significance as a messenger is confirmed in Surah 17:3: he is “a grateful servant” — a description that, in the Qur’an, connects thankfulness (shukr) with faith. To be ungrateful is a form of denial of Allah; to be grateful is a form of worship.

The Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham)

Ibrahim is the most important of the earlier prophets in Islam. He is described in Surah 37:109–111 as receiving Allah’s “peace and salutations” because he proved faithful, and as one who “tended always towards good deeds.” He is known as Khalilullah — the “Friend of Allah.”

Ibrahim’s story involves multiple tests. He was raised in a community of idol-worshippers — including his own father, who made idols. Ibrahim recognised the absurdity of worshipping created objects and challenged his community. In Surah 21:57–58, he is described as destroying the idols of his people, leaving only the largest standing so that people would have to ask “who did this?” — a dramatic act designed to make people think critically about what they were worshipping.

With his wife Hajra (Hajra) and son Ismail, Ibrahim established the sacred site of Makkah. In Surah 2:127–129, Ibrahim and Ismail together raise the foundations of the Ka’ba and pray: “Our Lord, accept this service from us… Our Lord, make us Muslims submitting to you, and of our descendants a Muslim nation submitting to you.” The prayer is answered in the community of Islam itself.

Ibrahim is also commanded to sacrifice his son. The Qur’an does not name which son in the sacrifice narrative itself (Surah 37:99–111). Most Muslim scholars traditionally identify the son as Ismail rather than Isaac (as in Genesis 22), based on the context of the narrative which places Ibrahim in the land of Makkah with Ismail. However, some Muslim scholars across history have argued it was Isaac, following the identification of the earlier revelation in the Tawrat. The debate is acknowledged in the spec. At the moment of sacrifice, Allah intervenes and ransoms the son with a great sacrifice — both are spared. This event is commemorated annually in Id-ul-Adha.

Key Fact

The Qur’an does not name the son in Ibrahim’s sacrifice (Surah 37). Most Muslim scholars traditionally identify him as Ismail based on context (Ibrahim is in Makkah with Ismail when this happens). Some scholars, however, have argued it was Isaac. The spec notes this as a “possible debate” — students should know both positions without asserting that the Qur’an definitively says one or the other.

The Prophet Ismail

Ismail is mentioned in Surah 21:5–86 among the earlier prophets. His characteristics as described in the Qur’an include patience and perseverance. He is also described as obedient to his parents and as commanding his family to pray and give zakah. In the Ka’ba-building narrative (Surah 2:127–129), he works alongside his father, symbolising both physical labour in service of Allah and the passing of faith from one generation to the next.

Ismail’s place in the prophetic chain is significant: Islamic tradition holds that Muhammad descended from Ismail through the Arab line, fulfilling the prayer Ibrahim and Ismail made when building the Ka’ba: “Send among them a messenger from among them.” Ismail thus links the story of Ibrahim to the coming of the Prophet Muhammad.

Key Fact

Nuh’s defining virtue is shukr (gratitude), shown in Surah 17:3. Ibrahim’s Ka’ba prayer (Surah 2:127–129) explicitly asks Allah to “send among them a messenger from among them” — Muslims understand this fulfilled in Muhammad. The son in the sacrifice (Surah 37) is unnamed; most classical Muslim scholars identify him as Ismail, but the debate exists and examiners award marks for acknowledging it.

The Prophet Yusuf (Joseph)

Yusuf’s story is told in Surah 12 — the only surah of the Qur’an devoted entirely to one prophet’s life. The opening verse calls it “the best of stories.” The narrative is rich with human emotion: jealousy, betrayal, temptation, imprisonment, patience, forgiveness and reunion.

Yusuf has the gift of dream interpretation. His brothers, jealous of their father’s love for him, throw him into a well and lie to their father Jacob, telling him Yusuf was eaten by a wolf. Yusuf is found by a passing caravan and taken to Egypt where he is bought as a slave. He is wrongly accused and imprisoned, but his faith and patience sustain him. In prison he interprets the dreams of fellow prisoners correctly.

Pharaoh has a dream that no one can interpret. Yusuf’s ability is remembered, and he interprets it: seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh releases and honours him, placing him in charge of Egypt’s food stores. The famine brings his brothers to Egypt seeking food. After a series of tests, Yusuf reveals himself and forgives them: “No reproach on you this day; Allah forgives you, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.”

Each prophet embodies a virtue that Muslims are called to imitate. Nuh: perseverance and gratitude despite near-total rejection. Ibrahim: courage, rational faith and total submission to Allah even when it costs everything. Ismail: patient obedience across generations. Yusuf: moral integrity under pressure, patience in suffering, and generous forgiveness of those who wronged him. The Qur’an repeatedly draws explicit lessons from these stories for the current reader, using the phrase “in this is a sign for those who reflect.”

The prophet stories also emphasise that prophets were human beings, not divine. They suffered, they wept, they were tested. This is important for Islamic theology: the prophets are honoured and their example is followed, but they are not worshipped. Only Allah is worthy of worship (Tawhid). Venerating a prophet to the point of directing worship to them would itself be a form of shirk.

Many of the Qur’anic prophet stories have parallels in the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament. Muslims believe the Qur’an is the final, uncorrupted revelation — where the Bible’s version differs, the Qur’an provides the authoritative account. The key differences in these four prophets include: Nuh’s son who dies (not in Genesis); Ibrahim’s idol-smashing (not in Genesis); the identification of the sacrifice son as Ismail (Genesis says Isaac); Yusuf’s moral emphasis on forgiveness and gratitude to Allah (which echoes the Genesis narrative very closely — one of the clearest instances of the Torah being confirmed by the Qur’an). Muslims use the term Tawrat for the Torah, acknowledging it as an earlier divine revelation while affirming that the Qur’an is the final, preserved revelation.
before.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers four prophets — know the surah reference for each: Nuh (Surah 71), Ibrahim (Surah 37:109–111; 2:127–129; 21:57–58), Ismail (Surah 21:5–86; 2:127–129), Yusuf (Surah 12). For the 5-mark source question, citing the surah earns the mark: “In Surah 2:127–129, Ibrahim and Ismail together build the Ka’ba…” For questions on the sacrifice, acknowledge the debate: most Muslim scholars say Ismail, but the Qur’an does not name him — this nuance earns marks at the top level. SPaG: use the Islamic names (Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail, Yusuf) not the biblical names (Noah, Abraham, Ishmael, Joseph) when answering on the Qur’an — but you can mention the biblical name in brackets to show your knowledge of both traditions.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Nuh (Surah 71) is the prophet of perseverance and gratitude; his son’s death by drowning shows that faith, not family, defines the community of believers.
  • Ibrahim (Surah 37; 2:127–129) is ‘Friend of Allah’ who builds the Ka’ba with Ismail; his sacrifice command is central to Id-ul-Adha — most Muslim scholars identify the son as Ismail, though the Qur’an does not name him.
  • Yusuf (Surah 12) — the only surah wholly devoted to one prophet — tells ‘the best of stories’: dreams, betrayal, prison, patience and ultimate forgiveness model the Muslim virtues of trust in Allah and generosity towards enemies.

glossary_terms.definition: Prophets and messengers sent by Allah throughout history to guide humanity; Islam recognises 25 named in the Qur'an and many more unnamed.
The prophet known as Noah in the Bible; called by Allah to warn his people, he built an ark to survive the flood; described as thankful (shakur) to Allah in Surah 17:3.
The prophet known as Abraham in the Bible; called 'the Friend of Allah' (Khalilullah), he is the ancestor of both Arabs and Jews and is central to Islamic faith.
Hagar in the Bible — the mother of Ismail; left by Ibrahim in the desert of Makkah, her desperate search for water is commemorated in the Hajj ritual of Sa'y.
The cubic black-clothed structure at the centre of the Masjid al-Haram in Makkah, considered the most sacred site in Islam; Muslims face it in prayer.
The prophet known as Ishmael in the Bible; the son of Ibrahim and Hajra, who helped build the Ka'ba and whose descendants include the Prophet Muhammad.
The prophet known as Joseph in the Bible; the subject of Surah 12 (Yusuf), the only Qur'anic surah devoted entirely to one prophet's story.
Yusuf's God-given ability to interpret the meaning of dreams; central to his story in Surah 12 and the means by which he rises from prison to power.

lessons.title: Dawud, Maryam, Isa and the Mission of Muhammad

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Qur'an says about the Prophet Dawud.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Dawud defeated Goliath (Jalut) in battle by Allah's leave, and was given the kingdom and wisdom (Surah 2:249-251).
• Dawud was given the Zabur (Psalms) as a revelation from Allah (Surah 17:55).
• Allah taught Dawud to make armour — his craftsmanship is described as a divine gift.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Surah 19 (Maryam) says about the annunciation and birth of Isa.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Jibril appeared to Maryam and announced that Allah would give her a pure son — she asked how this was possible since no man had touched her.
• Jibril replied 'Your Lord says it is easy for Me; We will make him a sign to the people.'
• When Maryam presented the newborn Isa to her people, he spoke from the cradle, declaring himself a servant and prophet of Allah.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Islamic teaching about Isa in Surah 4:157-158 differs from the Christian understanding.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• In Christianity, Jesus died on the cross and rose from the dead — the crucifixion is the central act of salvation. In Islam, Surah 4:157-158 states Isa was not killed or crucified; Allah raised him before death occurred — crucifixion is therefore not the basis of salvation in Islam.
• Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God who died to atone for human sin. In Islam, Isa is a great prophet and servant of Allah — born of a virgin, performing miracles — but not divine; his death (avoided by raising) is not understood as an atoning sacrifice.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Maryam is an important figure in Islam.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Maryam is the only woman named in the Qur'an and has an entire surah (Surah 19) named after her — this unique honour places her among the greatest figures in Islamic tradition, held up as a model of purity, faith and total submission to Allah's will.
• Maryam's experience of the annunciation and miraculous birth of Isa demonstrates Allah's unlimited creative power — 'Your Lord says it is easy for Me' (Surah 19) — and affirms that Allah can act outside natural processes when he chooses; this is a sign for believers.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 19 (Maryam) as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Muslims should not try to convert other people to Islam in modern Britain.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support (of the statement): Humanists argue that everyone has the right to their own beliefs and that attempting to convert others shows disrespect for religious freedom. In a pluralistic society, imposing one religion's truth claims risks division and harm. Non-Muslims may find attempts at conversion unwelcome or pressurising. Secular law in Britain protects freedom of religion.
Against: The Qur'an commands Muhammad to 'warn your nearest kin' (Surah 26:213-217) — a divine obligation that Muslims believe applies to all believers. Sharing one's faith is not the same as compulsion; Surah 2:256 states 'there is no compulsion in religion.' Da'wah (invitation) based on gentle persuasion and good example is the Islamic model, not force. Isa foretold Muhammad (Surah 61:6), showing that prophets always invited others — it is part of the prophetic tradition. Many Muslims see their commitment to social justice and ethical living as a form of witness that respects others' freedom.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Qur'an says about the life and mission of the Prophet Isa.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Isa was born miraculously of the virgin Maryam without a human father, by Allah's direct command.
• Isa performed miracles — healing the blind and leper, and raising the dead — as signs of his prophetic authority.
• Isa foretold the coming of a final messenger called Ahmad (Muhammad) in Surah 61:6.

before.exam_tip_html: The most sensitive exam question in this lesson concerns Surah 4:157–158. Always present it as an Islamic theological position, not as a historical claim: “In Islamic belief, the Qur’an teaches that Isa was not crucified but raised to Allah…” Do not phrase it as though you are adjudicating between Christianity and Islam. The 5-mark source question will likely ask about Isa or Maryam — cite the surah: “In Surah 19 (Maryam), Jibril announces the birth of Isa to Maryam…” For 12-mark Discuss questions, the non-religious argument (Humanist view on preaching, or visionary experiences not being proof of God) must be developed with genuine reasons, not just mentioned. SPaG: spell ‘Maryam’ (not Mary), ‘Jibril’ (not Gabriel) and ‘annunciation’ correctly in answers about the Qur’an.
